sources.supports: Rouille said roo-EE, French for rust, 'aioli's red cousin', garlic, chili and a pinch of saffron pounded with bread soaked in fish broth and mounted with olive oil, often with a yolk; aioli as the garlic sauce of Provence; preserved lemon standing in for part of the lemon juice in an aioli; terrines as seasoned meat, fish or vegetable mixtures cooked in a mold and served cold; fish drying past 63°C (145°F); Escoffier (1846 to 1935).

sources.title: Charte de la Bouillabaisse
sources.publisher: Office Métropolitain de Tourisme et des Congrès de Marseille
sources.supports: The charter was created in 1980 against restaurants that did not respect the traditional recipes, and sets out the ingredients of a quality bouillabaisse while respecting the professional's art. A Marseille bouillabaisse holds at least four species from: rascasse, baudroie (lotte), rascasse blanche, fielas (congre), araignée (vive), chapon (scorpène), galinette (rouget grondin, optional) and Saint-Pierre. The service is left to the restaurateur. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

The English page gives the chapon as 'capon (red scorpion fish)' and the galinette as red mullet, optional. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Bouillabaisse
sources.supports: A complex fish soup that began on the Mediterranean coast of France and a signature of Provençal cooking; the Marseille version is held the most authentic; ingredients: fish and shellfish, olive oil, onions, tomatoes, garlic, parsley, saffron, fennel, thyme, bay leaf and orange peel; it must use Mediterranean fish, with rascasse, a bony rock fish, essential; it is boiled quickly; rouille is a condiment added at the table, a paste of garlic, red pepper, bread crumbs and fish stock. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Bouillabaisse
sources.supports: The name explained from the method (the fish added one kind at a time and the pot brought to the boil); in 1980 eleven Marseille restaurateurs drew up the charter that codified ingredients and method; it must include rascasse (Scorpaena scrofa), 'a bony rockfish which lives in the calanque and reefs close to shore'; in Marseille restaurants the fish are cleaned, scaled and washed, the broth is served first, very hot, with rouille on thick slices of bread rubbed with garlic, and the fish and potatoes follow on a separate platter; some variations add orange peel. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Jean-Baptiste Reboul
sources.supports: A chef and the author of La Cuisinière provençale: more than 1,000 Provençal recipes and 365 menus; first edition 1897, an instant success; 24 editions and 250,000 copies; also titled La Cuisinière du Midi; still reprinted. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Aioli, and L'Aiòli (the newspaper)
sources.supports: Aioli is a compound of the Provençal ai, garlic, and oli, oil; the name means garlic and oil in Catalan and Provençal; 'true aioli contains garlic and no other seasoning (except salt)'. The page on L'Aiòli: Frédéric Mistral founded the Provençal language newspaper of that name in 1891, named for the dish. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Bouillabaisse Essentials
sources.supports: Olive oil, garlic and onions go into the pot with fennel tops and herbs; potatoes and tomatoes (fresh in season, otherwise canned) are added; 'Fish, whole or cut into pieces, is then put in (the firmer fish first, more delicate varieties on top)'; stock and more oil; 'rapid boiling is the key to the process, emulsifying the oil, stock, and fish gelatin'; 'this can take up to 25 minutes, depending on age of potatoes'; saffron is essential and tints soup and fish red orange; baguette rounds are toasted and rubbed with fresh garlic, spread with rouille at the table and set in the empty bowls for the broth; rouille is 'a garlicky mayonnaise with saffron' and there is 'no definitive recipe for rouille'. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Bouillabaisse (recipe), with True Bouillabaisse
sources.supports: Onions, crushed garlic, parsley, thyme, bay leaf and fennel in 1/4 cup of the oil in a 10 to 12 quart pot; large, whole and firm fish first, then smaller, more delicate fish; 'Strain soup, and, for the first course, spread rouille on toast, place 3 pieces in each warm soup bowl, and add soup'; the fish follows as the second course. True Bouillabaisse (saveur.com/article/Travels/True-Bouillabaisse): the oil, stock and fish gelatin in the pot emulsify into a rich broth. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Panisse Is Here to Replace Your French Fries
sources.supports: A local culinary historian: 'Panisse probably originated in Genoa, Italy, and was embraced and prepared in Nice before making its way to Marseille'; both cities claim it; in Nice it is sold in a round saucer shape, coffee saucers being the molds; in Marseille the batter is rolled in a towel into a cylinder and circles are cut and fried; a Nice cook says it should be chickpea flour only, and a packaged product was found listing wheat flour. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Three accounts of the 1980 charter: Generation Voyage (the origins 'from ancient Greece to the charter of 1980'), Perfectly Provence and Take a Chef
sources.publisher: Generation Voyage; Perfectly Provence; Take a Chef
sources.supports: One of them says the charter also requires saffron in threads and not powder, a rouille made in house and the broth served apart from the fish, and that it is a moral commitment among its signatories and not an official label; they count the drafters differently, eleven (perfectlyprovence.co) and about fifteen (takeachef.com/blog/fr-fr/meilleure-bouillabaisse-marseille). The summary did not say which page carried which sentence. A newspaper article in the same results (South China Morning Post, 'Marseille's beloved bouillabaisse gets update', scmp.com/lifestyle/food-drink/article/2125842) is read by its title only. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Three accounts of the name: a French dictionary page, a Marseille history article and a regional site
sources.publisher: La langue française (dictionary pages); Made in Marseille; Provence 7
sources.supports: The dictionary page: pronounced [bujabɛs], feminine noun, the spelling 'bouille à baisse' dated 1837, from the Provençal bouiabaisso, perhaps an alteration of 'bouille peis' (boil, fish) or from boil and lower. Made in Marseille (the address given here): Mistral gave the first plausible reading, 'boui abaisso', when it boils you lower it. Provence 7 lists the readings side by side: lower the boil, boil the fish, that which boils low. The dictionary page is on lalanguefrancaise.com; its exact address was not kept in the notes, so the address given here is the Marseille article. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Pages on the hard boil and the emulsion
sources.publisher: Recipe and teaching pages in one search (MasterClass, Obviously French and others)
sources.supports: 'Rapid boiling forces the olive oil into tiny droplets suspended in water, which creates a creamy texture further enhanced by the gelatin from the fish bones'; the gelatin of rascasse bones gives silkiness; one reference traces the name to a phrase meaning reduced broth and calls it a reminder that rapid boiling is needed to emulsify the large amount of oil. Against them, in the same results: one page warns that a boiled stock turns murky, one says the fish should poach at a simmer, and one account lowers the heat once the fish is in. The summary did not pin each sentence to its page. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: French pages on the method and the quantities

sources.supports: The fish is cooked in boiling water and plenty of olive oil until the broth is smooth and emulsified; one recipe takes 1.5 kg of firm fleshed sea fish for four people; there is no fixed recipe and it varies by family (provence-alpes-cotedazur.com/en/provence/things-to-do/wine-and-gastronomy/bouillabaisse-de-marseille-recipe/; routard.com/fr/mag/dossier/a/recette-de-la-bouillabaisse). The summary did not pin each sentence to its page. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.supports: A plated restaurant bouillabaisse: fish set on the plate with three potato balls, fennel salad and fennel fronds, a saffron jelly set with agar and fish stock, and grilled sourdough with rouille; the rouille is whisked slowly so that it thickens and does not split. sources.title: Fish in bouillabaisse sauce (recipe sheet)
sources.supports: A dish by that name: fennel, onion, garlic, potato and fish are cooked, cooled, blended for a few minutes, thinned with water if too thick, and strained; the list carries fennel seeds, white wine and Pernod. A cook's own site, so a weak source: it shows that the idea exists, not how any restaurant does it. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: The classic base and its arguments
sources.publisher: delicious. magazine and a recipe page in the same search
sources.supports: The classic base is olive oil, onions, garlic, fennel, tomatoes, saffron and a bouquet garni; orange peel and pastis are common additions and the other ingredients are 'the subject of heated debate'; one recipe calls pastis a Marseille ingredient in a Marseille dish, reinforcing the fennel and saffron. The summary did not pin each sentence to its page. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: French fish names in English
sources.publisher: Behind the French Menu, with a recipe on ckbk built on the charter
sources.supports: Vive is the weever; congre is the conger eel, fielas in Marseille, and the head of a conger sometimes goes into the pot; baudroie or lotte is the monkfish, also called anglerfish; Saint-Pierre is the John Dory, among the most delicate fish and usually added late; grondin is the sea robin in most sources and rouget grondin the red gurnard. The ckbk recipe (app.ckbk.com/recipe/simp30798c02s001r003/bouillabaisse) gives the galinette as red gurnard. The summary did not pin each name to its page. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: La rouille, la sauce solaire qui donne du caractère aux plats de la mer
sources.supports: The strict base is garlic, chili (cayenne or dried), saffron and olive oil, with bread crumb or potato as the binder; egg yolk is not indispensable, some modern recipes add it and others use cooked potato; the sauce must thicken and take a fine orange color. A recipe page in the same search says the name comes from the red orange color. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Rouille pages in English
sources.supports: A Provençal garlic, saffron and chili sauce traditionally served with bouillabaisse and fish soup, spread on croutons, orange red from saffron and peppers; Marseille thickens it with bread and Nice with egg yolks in the manner of a mayonnaise; it is 'usually thickened with bread or sometimes potato pulp'; the traditional version takes saffron as its main aromatic and modern ones often use red pepper, pimentón or cayenne; one page calls the base an aioli with chilies and a little paprika; one says it is not a garnish but part of the dish (foodrepublic.com/1544787/what-is-rouille-difference-aioli/; mashed.com/605579/what-is-rouille-and-how-is-it-used; beyond.fr/food/rouille.html). The summary did not pin each sentence to its page. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: A rouille made by hand
sources.publisher: A recipe page in one search (the Saveur gallery Making Bouillabaisse or Obviously French)
sources.supports: Anchovy, saffron and bread soaked in broth are pounded to a thick paste; egg yolks and cayenne are added; the olive oil goes in drop by drop at first, then in a slow stream. The summary did not say which of the two pages carried it. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: aioli

sources.title: The chickpea cooking of the south of France
sources.publisher: The Good Life France, with a recipe on ckbk for the whole family (cade, calentica, farinata, panisse, socca)
sources.supports: Socca is baked in a wood fired oven on a hot flat pan as a very thin pancake; panisse is cooked to a firm paste, cooled until it can be cut, and deep fried. The ckbk recipe (its id there is plag22408c09s001r009) takes 400 g of chickpea flour to 80 cl of water, twice as thick as the panisse recipes, and one chef there credits chickpea flour cooking to Liguria. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Panisse recipes
sources.publisher: Snippets of Paris; Mission Food Adventure; one more recipe site
sources.supports: About 250 g of chickpea flour to 1 liter of water (Snippets of Paris; a second, a food writer's own site, gives the same and is left unnamed because its address is the writer's name); sifted flour whisked into simmering water to a thick batter, poured into a greased dish and set for a few hours in the refrigerator, then cut and fried; other recipes add cold water to the flour; a little olive oil or butter in the batter helps prevent lumps. No page gave a frying temperature. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Authentiques panisses de Marseille, with Panisses farcis à l'anchois

sources.title: Cooking Mousselines, and Basic Mousseline Formula, in a garde manger textbook on ckbk

sources.title: Teaching pages on mousse, mousseline and quenelle

sources.title: Pages on cooking and pressing a fish terrine
sources.publisher: Kitchen NMBRS (a Dutch kitchen reference) and two recipe pages in the same search
sources.supports: Oven 150 to 160°C for fish terrines, a core of 62 to 65°C, 4 to 8 hours of pressing; cover and chill at least 4 hours, preferably overnight; fish to at least 145°F (63°C) by a food safety page; a fish loaf can turn rubbery, a gentle water bath avoids toughness, and water at a boil lets steam into the mold unevenly. sources.title: Confit fennel recipes
sources.publisher: olive magazine; Amazing Food Made Easy; Oliso; two recipe pages
sources.supports: 'The slices are submerged in olive oil and slowly cooked with lemon zest, garlic and fresh herbs. It's a low and slow cooking method that produces food with a silky texture and concentrated flavor.' One recipe cooks cut fennel with garlic in olive oil and butter at 140°C for about 2 hours until soft; olive magazine cuts 500 g of fennel into 12 wedges; sous vide versions hold 183°F (83.9°C) or 185°F, one of them titled Orange-Saffron Fennel Confit; it keeps up to 3 days refrigerated and the strained oil up to a month; tarragon amplifies the anise note. sources.title: Genetics, genomics and breeding of fennel (review, 2025)
sources.publisher: BMC Plant Biology, on PubMed Central
sources.supports: The species name is still debated: Linnaeus first named the plant Anethum foeniculum, for its high content of anethole, and the authors keep the classical name Foeniculum vulgare. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Three papers on the chemistry and grading of saffron
sources.publisher: Digital Library of Slovenia (a journal paper); Encyclopedia.pub (entry 34202); a Royal Society of Chemistry supplement
sources.supports: Crocin is the carotenoid behind the yellow orange color, measured by absorbance at 440 nm; picrocrocin gives the bitter taste and is the second most abundant component of the dry spice; safranal is the volatile behind the smell and forms mainly from picrocrocin as the spice dries. The papers describe the grades of ISO 3632 differently, three in one and four categories in another (rsc.org/suppdata/c5/ay/c5ay01986a/c5ay01986a1.pdf). Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Two figures for the flowers behind a kilogram of saffron
sources.supports: About 150,000 flowers for 1 kg by the first; the stigmas of 1,500 flowers for 1 g by the second (encyclopedia.com/plants-and-animals/plants/plants/saffron), which is ten times as many. The two do not agree. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Pages on preserved lemon
sources.publisher: A recipe wiki drawn from Wikipedia; Morocco World News; the Montreal Gazette (2019); Good Food (Australia); a Moroccan recipe page
sources.supports: A salt cured lemon condiment common in North African cooking, Moroccan above all, used in tagines, sauces and salads and with fish and chicken; whole lemons packed with coarse salt; one recipe takes 6 lemons of about 140 g, 6 more for juice and 3/4 cup (110 g) of kosher salt, shaken now and then 'for at least 3 weeks, until lemon rinds soften'; 'Traditionally, they'd be pickled for several weeks'; a quick version takes 48 hours; one page says the pulp is not usually used and it is the peel that is eaten, another uses pulp and skin together; the taste is 'Tart, briny and surprisingly complex'. The summary did not pin each sentence to its page. Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

sources.title: Preserved Lemon Aioli
sources.supports: A published recipe: 1/4 cup of preserved lemon chopped coarse, 3 large egg yolks, garlic and vegetable oil (not olive), with lemon juice added at the end, and a note that it is made with raw egg. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Other preserved lemon aioli recipes
sources.publisher: Food52; Today; a recipe from an Australian cafe on Clove Kitchen; Unilever Food Solutions
sources.supports: One is offered for any seafood and starts with an egg yolk and a neutral oil before olive oil is whisked in slowly; one purees mayonnaise with preserved lemon, garlic, water, cayenne and olive oil and serves it with pan cooked cod (today.com); one is called good with fish, baked potatoes or grilled asparagus and uses 2 yolks and white wine vinegar; a food service recipe pairs it with harissa. So the sauce is common in published cooking and is put with fish and seafood. No page called the flavor floral. Read through a search summary; the page was not opened.

sources.title: Pages on bourride
sources.publisher: Tasting Table; a second page (TasteAtlas or a travel site); Saveur (Bourride, fish stew with aioli)
sources.supports: 'what differentiates bourride from the more famous bouillabaisse is the addition of aioli, a sauce made with garlic, olive oil, and, usually, egg yolks'; a saffron free recipe is dated to an 1897 cookbook that describes an aioli thickened bouillabaisse; bourride is the everyday fishers' stew, cheaper, of a single white fish, traditionally monkfish. A third page in the search says both stews are scented with saffron, garlic, fennel and orange peel, so the pages disagree on saffron in a bourride (saveur.com/article/recipes/classic-french-fish-stew-with-aioli). Found by the first researcher of this dish, whose notes survive; read through a search summary, the page not opened.

firstResearcher: # Bouillabaisse research notes (searches used so far: 1 of 18; WebFetch tried once, refused: ENOTFOUND)

S1 charter: 11 Marseille restaurateurs 1980; counter non-traditional restaurants (one source: mass tourism, frozen fish). Tourism office: at least 4 species from: rascasse, baudroie, congre (fielas), araignee (vive), chapon, Saint-Pierre; galinette optional (per summary). Served generally in two dishes, fish and broth; rouille with croutons. Moral commitment, not an official label. Carving before the guest NOT confirmed in S1.

URLs: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouillabaisse ; marseille-tourisme.com/offres/charte-de-la-bouillabaisse-marseille-2eme-fr-3383880/ ; marseille-tourisme.com/marseille/traditions/la-bouillabaisse/ ; generationvoyage.fr/bouillabaisse-marseille/ ; scmp.com/lifestyle/food-drink/article/2125842/... ; marseille-tourisme.com/en/r/leaflet/the-bouillabaisse-fish-soup

S2 etymology (2/18): Academie 9e ed (dictionnaire-academie.fr/article/A9B1728): XIXe siecle, forme "bouille baisse" (bouille baïsse); emprunte du provencal boui-abaisso, "bous et abaisse". Dictionary via lalanguefrancaise.com: [bujabɛs] n.f., "bouille à baisse" 1837; provenc. bouiabaisso, peut-etre alter. de bouille peis (bouillir + peis poisson) ou bouillir et abaisser. madeinmarseille.net/a-la-une-marseille/17202-histoire-bouillabaisse-cuisine-gastronomie/: Mistral first plausible: "boui abaisso" = quand ca bout tu baisses (not quoted from the Tresor). provence7.com lists several etymologies: bouiabaisso/bolhabaissa imperative lower the boil; boui peis boil the fish; qui bout en bas. en.wiktionary: Occitan possibly bolhir + abaissar. ckbk "Published 2004" reference bouillabaisse (app.ckbk.com/reference/food34962c19s001e095e005e003/bouillabaisse) not summarised.

S3 Reboul (3/18): 1st ed 1897 instant success; 24 editions 250,000 copies, also titled La Cuisiniere du Midi, still reprinted (en.wikipedia Jean-Baptiste_Reboul). Slate.fr /story/38753/bouillabaisse "Noble bouillabaisse": Reboul cites 40 fish usable. NatGeo (nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/bouillabaisse-deconstructing-pride-marseille): recipe became gospel for decades. Archive.org scan 1909 3rd ed exists. Recipe text NOT returned.

S4 method (4/18): name from method, fish added one at a time and brought to boil (Wikipedia). Other variations add orange peel. In Marseille restaurants bouillon served first very hot with rouille spread on thick slices of bread rubbed with garlic; fish and potatoes next on a separate platter. 1980 11 restaurateurs Charter codified ingredients and method. Must include rascasse, bony rockfish of calanques and reefs. Reboul dates NOT confirmed; emulsion NOT confirmed; marette NOT found.

S5 rouille FR (5/18): figaronautisme.meteoconsult.fr/actus-nautisme-lifestyle/2026-01-09/84354-la-rouille-la-sauce-solaire-qui-donne-du-caractere-aux-plats-de-la-mer : base stricte ail, piment (Cayenne ou sec), safran, huile d'olive, mie de pain ou pomme de terre comme liant; jaune d'oeuf pas indispensable, certaines recettes modernes l'ajoutent, d'autres pomme de terre cuite; doit epaissir, belle couleur orangee. croq-kilos.com recette: nom provient de sa couleur rouge orangee. OQLF (vitrinelinguistique.oqlf.gouv.qc.ca/fiche-gdt/fiche/8975358/aioli): aioli = sauce a base d'ail pile, de jaune d'oeuf et d'huile d'olive. Larousse NOT found.

S6 aioli (6/18): en.wikipedia Aioli: compound of Provencal ai garlic + oli oil; name means garlic and oil in Catalan and Provencal; "true aioli contains garlic and no other seasoning (except salt)". etymonline.com/word/aioli: garlic mayonnaise sense 1894. etymologist.ai ~1900 English; oli from Latin oleum. en.wikipedia L'Aiòli: Mistral founded Provencal language newspaper 1891, Felibrige, named for the dish. marseille-tourisme.com/en/discover-marseille/gastronomy-in-marseille/aioli-of-marseille : Mistral published his personal aioli recipe in the Almanach provencal; purists garlic, olive oil, salt in a mortar; egg an addition in some regions and modern restaurant versions; some add lemon juice, breadcrumbs, potatoes or mustard.

S7 rouille EN (7/18): kvalifood.com/posts/rouille/: Provencal garlic saffron chili sauce traditionally served with bouillabaisse and fish soup; orange red colour from saffron and peppers; Marseille uses bread as thickener, Nice uses egg yolks mayonnaise style (which source? one of: kvalifood / foodrepublic / mashed). "usually thickened with bread or sometimes potato pulp" (beyond.fr/food/rouille.html?). one source: "composed of garlic, saffron or red chili peppers, breadcrumbs or potatoes, egg yolks, and olive oil" (recidemia?). Mustard in many not constant. foodrepublic.com/1544787/what-is-rouille-difference-aioli/ ; mashed.com/605579/what-is-rouille-and-how-is-it-used ; thetakeout.com/1995324/... ; thegoodlifefrance.com/recipe-for-rouille-a-taste-of-provence/ ; app.ckbk.com/recipe/thec18041c02s001r002/rouille

S8 panisse (8/18): marseille-tourisme.com/en/discover-marseille/gastronomy-in-marseille/panisses/ : Italian workers from Piedmont and Liguria who worked in the l'Estaque factories. saveur.com/panisse-provence-best-french-snack/ : local culinary historian: "Panisse probably originated in Genoa, Italy, and was embraced and prepared in Nice before making its way to Marseille"; both cities claim birthplace; in Nice sold in round saucer shape (coffee saucers as molds); in Marseille batter rolled in a towel into a cylinder, circles cut and fried; a Nice cook says should only be chickpea flour, a packaged product listed wheat flour. wikipedia Panissa: Ligurian name panissa; farinata in Liguria, socca in Nice, cade in Toulon (cade thicker with crunchy surface). Socca: baked in wood fired oven on hot flat pan, very thin pancake; panisse cooked to a firm paste, cooled till it can be cut, deep fried (thegoodlifefrance.com/chickpea-cuisine-of-the-south-of-france/). ckbk recipe plag22408c09s001r009 (Cade/Calentica/Farinata/Panisse/Socca): 400 g chickpea flour, 80 cl water. One chef attributes chickpea flour recipes to Liguria. davidlebovitz.com panisse recipe (living writer, do not name). mashed.com/1314649/chickpea-fries-parisian-street-food-menu.

S9 mousseline (9/18): ckbk Escoffier (esco04831) "1562 Forcemeat for Mousses and Mousselines of Fish" app.ckbk.com/recipe/esco04831c06s002r010/... and "fine forcemeat with cream known as mousseline forcemeat" app.ckbk.com/recipe/esco04831c02s002ss002r003/... ; ckbk "Basic Mousseline Formula" (gard79963, a Garde Manger titled book, not verified as CIA); ckbk "General Information About Fish Mousseline" (fund22556): "The proportions of ingredients for fish mousseline, a puree of fish with cream and egg whites, will vary depending on how you will use it and the type of fish selected"; for quenelles make a stronger one; terrine: increase egg whites or decrease cream; lean fish sole pike turbot need less egg white, watery fish more ("some other sole give off a lot of water when cooked and will require more egg white"). One classic formula: 250 g raw flesh, 250 ml cream, white of 1 egg and seasoning (source among results not pinned; dailymaverick or slideshare). A fish mousseline recipe: 1 cup whipping cream, cold. Shellfish crab, shrimp, prawn, lobster popular (slideshare chapter 16). Keep fish cold, cream chilled, chilled egg whites. theculinarypro.com/forcemeats. NOT confirmed: test quenelle, 170F bath, 145F internal, CIA.

S10 hard boil (10/18): several sources: vigorous boil emulsifies olive oil and fish fats into broth; "Rapid boiling forces the olive oil into tiny droplets suspended in water, which creates a creamy texture further enhanced by the gelatin from the fish bones" (recipe site, which? cuvvo.pages.dev or masterclass or obviouslyfrench); gelatin from rascasse bones gives silkiness. Name "often traced to a phrase meaning reduced broth, and a reminder that rapid boiling is needed to emulsify the large amount of oil" (ckbk reference food00011 "Soups and Stews; Bouillabaisse"? not pinned). saveur.com/article/Travels/True-Bouillabaisse: the oil, stock and fish gelatin in the pot emulsify into a rich, satisfying broth. DISAGREE: one source warns against boiling stock (murky); another says fish should poach at a simmer; one account: temperature lowered once fish went in, allowing it to poach; others: adding olive oil during boiling to emulsify is essential. Straining: through a fine sieve pressing hard on solids with back of spoon (gourmettraveller recipe?). NatGeo title "A fine meshed sieve". Fish order NOT found. thedailymeal.com/community/bourride-bouillabaisses-troubled-cousin exists (bourride). csmonitor 2010 "Fish stew, French style".

S11 terrine (11/18): ckbk gard79963 "Cooking Mousselines" (app.ckbk.com/section/gard79963c15s001ss004sss005/cooking-mousselines): "Molded mousselines and mousseline-based terrines are baked at low temperatures in a hot bain-marie, or water bath. They are always covered, usually with parchment and then aluminum foil."; "generally cooked to an internal temperature of 145F (62C), or until they are just set"; reach about 150F (65C) by carryover; oven 300F to 325F (150 to 163C) (same or another). kitchennmbrs.app/en/product-knowledge/technieken/terrine-bereiden table: 150 to 160C oven for fish terrines; fish core 62 to 65C; 4 to 8 hours pressing for fish terrines. Another: cover and chill minimum 4 hours, preferably overnight. Food safety source: at least 145F (63C). Faults: cold set fish loaves can turn rubbery; gentle bain-marie avoids toughness; water at a boil lets steam penetrate unevenly. ckbk reference food00011 "Mousselines, Quenelles". NOT found: grainy/broken, weeping, egg white rubbery.

S12 confit fennel (12/18): americastestkitchen.com/recipes/14406-fennel-confit (ATK). A recipe: cut fennel with garlic in olive oil and butter at 140C about 2 hours until soft (which? ffmm.squarespace or divaliciousrecipes). Sous vide: 183F (83.9C) amazingfoodmadeeasy.com "Sous Vide Orange-Saffron Fennel Confit"; another 185F (oliso.com). olivemagazine.com/recipes/vegetarian/confit-fennel-with-puy-lentils: 500 g fennel cut into 12 wedges. "The slices are submerged in olive oil and slowly cooked with lemon zest, garlic and fresh herbs. It's a low and slow cooking method that produces food with a silky texture and concentrated flavor." (withspice.com or oliso). Keeps refrigerated up to 3 days; strained oil up to one month (one source). Tarragon amplifies the anise notes. Anethole NOT found.

S13 saffron (13/18): britannica.com/topic/saffron: "golden-colored pungent stigmas (pollen-receiving structures) of the autumn crocus (Crocus sativus), which are dried and used as a spice to flavor foods and as a dye"; three orange stigmas of each flower collected and dried. encyclopedia.pub/entry/16790: about 150,000 flowers per 1 kg. encyclopedia.com/plants-and-animals/plants/plants/saffron: 1 g requires stigmata of 1500 flowers (=1.5 million per kg): tenfold conflict. NOT found: crocin, safranal, picrocrocin, anethole. Other hits not summarised: alimentarium.org saffron, mccormickscienceinstitute saffron.

S14 pairing (14/18): decanter.com/learn/best-wine-with-a-bouillabaisse-fish-stew-ask-decanter-455805: writer prefers Bandol rose over Cotes de Provence: "stronger flavoured and more savoury than many Cotes de Provence roses". vinatis.com/conseils/quel-vin-avec-la-bouillabaisse-: Bandol rose "ticks all the boxes" as opposed to a pale light summer glass. Cotes de Provence rose lighter option; one guide: cleanses the palate between bites (thekitchencommunity.org); French forum (lapassionduvin.com): Cotes de Provence rose to match the soup's spiciness. Cassis white = the classic accord with bouillabaisse (one source; hachette-vins.com/cuisine-vins/43/bouillabaisse/ or vinatis), another: acidity cuts through; Bandol white fuller than Cassis. Why: acidity cuts richness; acid lifts saffron broth and shellfish; aioli: irishexaminer.com/food/arid-41818091.html chilled Provence rose "one of the few things that can cut through the garlicky richness"; regional guide: Provencal rose fresh and fruity with a touch of minerality. avenuedesvins "quel vin boire avec un aioli". Minuty NOT covered.

S15 New Orleans (15/18): en.wikipedia Picayune_Creole_Cookbook: published New Orleans 1901, widely credited with preserving Creole cooking tradition; critics: diminished contributions of African, Caribbean, Native American. 1901 bouillabaisse recipe: slices of red snapper and redfish (ckbk thep19270 = The Picayune's Creole Cook Book, app.ckbk.com/recipe/thep19270c04s001ss004r006/bouillabaisse; foodhistory.com/classics/picayune/ccb.htm). One recipe page credits Thackeray with famous tribute to Creole cookery; another renders it: the likes of the New Orleans bouillabaisse were never eaten in Marseilles or Paris (wording varies, no primary citation). 1910 menu reprint: Redfish Bouillabaisse, Gulf fish in place of Mediterranean (oldtimyrecipes.blogspot). Commentary (davidsanfordshields.substack issue 44): tomato based court bouillon has become the norm in the 1901 edition. Ballad of Bouillabaisse NOT found. 64parishes.org/entry/cookbooks. archive.org scan cu31924073878708.
grep repo for preserved lemon sources before spending a search.

S16 bourride/cioppino (16/18): tastingtable.com/1386373/bourride-french-fish-stew-aioli-ingredient: "what differentiates bourride from the more famous bouillabaisse is the addition of aioli, a sauce made with garlic, olive oil, and, usually, egg yolks"; dates saffron free recipe to an 1897 cookbook describing an aioli thickened bouillabaisse without saffron (Reboul 1897 presumably, not named in summary). Another (tablejourney or tasteatlas.com/bourride): bourride everyday fisherman's stew in Marseille from 19th century, cheaper, single white fish; traditional fish monkfish (baudroie a la setoise). Third source (saveur quiz?): both scented with saffron, garlic, fennel and orange peel (conflict on saffron). Cioppino: harborfish.com/bouillabaisse-or-cioppino/: "while cioppino has a true tomato base, bouillabaisse has a white (fish stock) base with some tomatoes thrown in"; cioppino Italian American style fish stew invented in San Francisco (wikipedia Fish stew? or farmtojar); ehow: cioppino usually includes wine, traditionally red, white acceptable, wine contentious in bouillabaisse.

S17 sauce/plating (17/18): Classic base: olive oil, onions, garlic, fennel, tomatoes, saffron, bouquet garni; orange peel and pastis common additions, other ingredients "subject of heated debate" (deliciousmagazine.co.uk/recipes/bouillabaisse/ or saveur). One recipe: pastis "a Marseille ingredient in a Marseille dish, reinforcing the fennel and saffron". greatbritishchefs.com/recipes/bouillabaisse-recipe: stick blender to a smooth sauce, pour through a fine sieve pressing the solids with a ladle, then through a fine chinois without pressing. A recipe (thestaffcanteen.com/chefs-recipes/bouillabaisse-1647015783 or finedininglovers "secrets french cuisine bouillabaisse"): plated with 3 potato balls, fennel salad, fennel fronds, saffron jelly set with agar, grilled sourdough with rouille. La Mer style: fish soup in crust broken at the table (foodnetwork). Rouille "usually garlic, saffron and chilli mayonnaise. Not a garnish, part of the dish." Served broth and fish separately or one bowl. NOT found: reduce and mount with butter/oil; terrine version.

S18 preserved lemon (18/18, allowance spent): salt cured lemon condiment common in North African cooking, especially Moroccan; also known as "country lemon" and leems (recipes.fandom.com/wiki/Preserved_lemon, Wikipedia derived); used in tagines, sauces, salads; fish and chicken dishes; traditional: whole lemons packed with coarse salt; recipe: 6 lemons (about 5 oz or 140 g each) + 6 more for juicing with 3/4 cup (110 g) kosher salt (salimaskitchen.com or tasteofmaroc); "Shake gently occasionally, for at least 3 weeks, until lemon rinds soften"; another "Total Time: 3 weeks"; quick version 48 hours; "Traditionally, they'd be pickled for several weeks" (goodfood.com.au); part used: "The lemon pulp isn't usually used, it's the preserved peel..." vs "Fistfuls of the tender pulp and skin"; taste "Tart, briny and surprisingly complex", tangy salty. moroccoworldnews.com/2013/01/147056/moroccan-cuisine-how-to-make-preserved-lemons/ ; pressreader montreal-gazette 2019 "Preserved lemons add salty flair to dishes". Preserved lemon aioli NOT found.
secondResearcher: # Second researcher, restart. Continues from ../bouillabaisse/notes.md (18 searches there). New allowance 18.

N1 (1/18) charter FR: marseille-tourisme.com/offres/charte-de-la-bouillabaisse-marseille-2eme-fr-3383880/ : created 1980 "pour lutter contre le service de certains restaurants ne respectant pas les recettes de cuisine traditionnelles"; aims to specify ingredients of a quality bouillabaisse "tout en respectant l'art du professionnel". At least 4 species among: rascasse, baudroie (lotte), rascasse blanche, fielas (congre), araignee (vive), chapon (scorpene), galinette (rouget grondin, facultatif), Saint-Pierre. Service left to the restaurateur's appreciation (tourism office). Another site (generationvoyage or takeachef): saffron in pistils not powder, rouille made in house, broth served separately from the fish. Moral commitment, not official label. Drafters: six (slate.fr), eleven (perfectlyprovence.co), about fifteen (takeachef.com). Carving before the guest NOT found; full text NOT found.

N2 (2/18) Reboul: BnF catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb40043939j : "Reboul, Jean-Baptiste (1862-1926)", 2005 De Boree reprint with glossary and index. en.wikipedia Jean-Baptiste_Reboul: chef; book compiling over 1,000 Provencal recipes and 365 menus; first ed 1897 instant success. NatGeo: 1897 recipe "became gospel for decades", norm for much of 20th century until cheaper versions led to a scandal. Slate: forty fish. Saveur Bouillabaisse-Essentials (fisherman's recipe): olive oil, garlic, onions, fennel tops, thyme, herbs. A recipe guide: saffron and cayenne essential. britannica.com/topic/bouillabaisse exists (not summarised). Reboul's own ingredient list, orange peel, feu vif NOT found.

N3 (3/18) Thackeray: gutenberg.org/files/2732/2732-h/2732-h.htm Ballads by W. M. Thackeray includes The Ballad of Bouillabaisse; opening: "Rue Neuve des Petits Champs its name is, The New Street of the Little Fields" (literaryballadarchive.com transcription); poets.org/poem/ballad-bouillabaisse ; literaryballadarchive.com/?p=1794 "W. M. Thackeray 1811-63"; paperspast 1911: poem recalls dingy but cosy little restaurant in that street where he first sampled it. Year NOT found; "A Mississippi Bubble"/Pontchartrain NOT found.

N4 (4/18) rouille dictionary: no dictionary page returned. Cooking sites: Provencal sauce of garlic, chili, saffron, traditionally with bouillabaisse and fish soup, spread on croutons; one: base often an aioli with chilies and a little paprika; name from its orange red colour (saffron and peppers); traditional uses saffron as main aromatic, modern often red peppers, pimenton or cayenne. glorious-food-glossary.com/cms/glossary/51-glossary-r/2165-rouille.html ; beyond.fr/food/rouille.html ; routard.com recette-de-la-bouillabaisse.

N5 (5/18) rouille dictionaries (allowed domains): dictionnaire-academie.fr/article/A9R3069 (9e ed): "Sauce provencale de couleur rouge orange, a base d'huile d'olive, d'ail, de piment rouge ou de safran, que l'on sert avec la bouillabaisse ou la soupe de poissons." larousse.fr/dictionnaires/francais/rouille/70030: "Sorte d'aioli releve, accompagnant la soupe de poisson et la bouillabaisse." dictionnaire.lerobert.com/en/definition/bouillabaisse: "souvent presentee avec des croutons et une sauce aillee, appelee rouille, qu'on peut y diluer". oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100430470 (Rouille): red chillies, garlic, olive oil, breadcrumbs or potatoes to bind; "The chillis give it a brownish-red colour, whence its name (French rouille means literally 'rust')."
